nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_000
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are the two most popular business models in the dress rental market?
nodes.answer: The two most popular business models in the dress rental market are short-term dress rental and subscription rental platforms, making up an estimated 90% of the market.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_001
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What measures can businesses in the fashion rental industry take to facilitate their recovery?
nodes.answer: Businesses in the fashion rental sector may need to adapt their business models, enhance hygiene practices, and implement innovative marketing strategies to regain consumer trust and stimulate demand.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_002
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What economic impacts can be expected by transitioning the fashion industry to a distributed production model?
nodes.answer: Transitioning the fashion industry to a distributed production model can have economic impacts such as opening up to new investors, enhancing competitiveness, and creating new job opportunities and value creation.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_003
nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: Are companies effectively embracing these sufficiency-driven strategies?
nodes.answer: The results show that while adoption is gaining momentum, companies often start with strategies that have less impact on their traditional operations.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_004
nodes.label: Science and Tech
nodes.question: What is the key feature of Faraday-Usta's hierarchical challenge analysis approach for servicing business models?
nodes.answer: The key feature of Faraday-Usta's hierarchical challenge analysis approach is its basis in a novel eutrophic set, which is used to analyse servicing business models.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_005
nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: What are some of the barriers that companies face when trying to transition towards a more steady-state or slowed-down economy?
nodes.answer: Companies face challenges such as a competitive business environment, pressure to maximize short-term shareholder value, concerns about global effects of stagnation, and affordability issues.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_006
nodes.label: Factual
nodes.question: What are the potential consequences for companies who continue to rely on outdated business models that may be considered 'out of fashion'?
nodes.answer: Companies that persist in outdated business models risk alienating increasingly conscious stakeholders and losing credibility, potentially leading to negative impacts on their prospects and overall success in the market.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_007
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How do Brocken and Short propose businesses can develop sustainable business model archetypes?
nodes.answer: Brocken and Short propose that businesses can develop sustainable business model archetypes by conducting a literature and practice review to understand and identify common patterns and strategies that lead to sustainable business practices.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_008
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: How many different main enterprise types are included in the value chain model?
nodes.answer: The value chain model consists of 16 different main enterprise types.
nodes.paragraph: These parameters were used as inputs in the value chain module that describe the flow of seafood products from fishers to consumers and the associated rev - enues, costs, salaries, and employment for all stakeholders in the value chain (Christensen et al. 2011). The value chain model consisted of 16 different main enterprise types, whose main linkages are depicted in Fig. 2 (see Supplementary material 2.1 for more information on the data for the value chain). The value chain structure was defined using previous fish value chain reports developed in Spain (Tragsatec 2011, 2012a, b, C; Garc a Antoni 2012; EUMOFA 2015; Cam 2020 ; Ortega Cerd and Coll 2022a ; Ortega Cerd et al. 2023; Ram rez and Sarroca 2023; Moranta et al. 2023) and was checked to ensure fulfilness and adequacy in fora with the participation of the main stakeholders of the area (Mas- carell-Rocher 2021; Ortega Cerd and Coll 2022b; Ortega Cerd et al. 2023). Most of the value chain operates as a fresh supply chain within the national market, with very low processing levels.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Circular economy initiatives|Adoption of circular business models_qna_009
nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: How might a bank's business model influence its response to economic recovery efforts?
nodes.answer: A bank's willingness to support economic recovery can vary based on its business model, ownership structures, and resulting objective functions.
nodes.paragraph: Limiting the negative economic consequences of future natural hazard shocks is therefore an urgent and high-priority policy goal (Koubi, 2019; United Nations, 2015). It is widely acknowledged that the banking sector has an important role to play in this endeavour (Carney, 2015; Ranger et al., 2021; United Nations, 2023). By facilitating access to finance, banks can enhance economic resilience through critical times and contribute to sustained economic growth and employment participation across societal groups. This is particularly true for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and otherwise underserved and excluded populations, which are highly vulnerable to exogenous shocks. However, the relationship between natural hazards, banks, and real economic resilience is more complex than this. First, banks themselves can be negatively impacted and experience losses and threats to their financial health, potentially limiting the ability to supply recovery loans. Second, banks may differ in their willingness to support economic recovery based on their business models, ownership structures, and resulting objective functions (Beck et al., 2018; Brei & Schclarek, 2015).
